--- title: "13 — Tracking a drifting DARM parameter" description: "The DARM loop's calibration parameters drift, forcing continuous re-measurement. On the coupled reduced-quad plant, track an actuation strength κ(t), the SRC detuning δ(t) (which splits the cavity pole into a complex pair), and finally several parameters drifting at once under a realistic random wander — recovered jointly with Lataire–Pintelon fits on leakage-free P&S snapshots, within honest Cramér–Rao bands, with the correlation matrix exposing which drifts are degenerate." image: thumbnails/13.svg categories: [calibration, closed-loop, DARM, time-varying] freeze: true --- ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## What you'll learn - Why a *drifting* plant is a system-ID problem, not a re-measurement chore. - Recovering a time-varying actuation strength **κ(t)** from leakage-free snapshots, with a real CRB. - Tracking the **SRC detuning δ(t)** — the *new* physics of the coupled plant, where the cavity pole splits into a complex pair — from the Pcal FRF, independent of the κ drift. - Tracking **several parameters drifting at once, at random** (a joint fit), and reading off from the **correlation matrix** which drifts are hard to tell apart. - Proving each drift is **resolvable** with a computed bound — not eyeballing the plot. ::: The [DARM calibration page](08-darm-calibration.qmd) recovers the loop's sensing, actuation, and response at **one instant**. But the reason DARM calibration is the slowest recurring LIGO measurement is that those parameters **drift** — the optical gain, the coupled-cavity pole, and the actuation strengths wander over minutes to hours, so the calibration is re-measured again and again. This page treats that drift head-on: as a slowly time-varying system to *identify*, not a nuisance to average away. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## The plant and the scope This runs on the **new coupled DARM plant** — the M0-damped reduced-QUAD hierarchical actuation (M0 / PUM / ESD) with coupled detuned-cavity sensing, where the SRC detuning splits the cavity pole into a complex pair (the same twin as [example 08](08-darm-calibration.qmd)). We build up in three steps: a single actuation strength κ(t) on a smooth curve, then the SRC detuning δ(t), then the realistic case — **several parameters drifting at once, at random**, recovered jointly. Still deferred: a Gaussian-process wander with a measured drift spectrum, all seven TDCFs together, and the one-shot (rather than two-step) Lataire–Pintelon fit. Rendered with `freeze: true`. ::: ::: {#48e6009d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import darm_tv_demo as dd from IPython.display import display ``` ::: ## The idea: locally stationary snapshots The plant drifts far more slowly than one measurement record (an hour-scale drift versus a ~16 s record), so within any single record it is **locally stationary** — the Pintelon–Schoukens picture of a linear model around a slowly-moving operating point. That licenses a two-step estimator: 1. **Snapshot.** At a sequence of times, take one leakage-free periodic-multisine measurement and recover the instantaneous actuation strength with **Pcal as the ruler**. Because the sensing `C` cancels in the stage-to-Pcal ratio, each snapshot is *immune to sensing drift* and carries an honest per-estimate σ. 2. **Basis fit.** Fit `κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a time-basis (Legendre) to the snapshot series by weighted least squares — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion in two-step form. The coefficient covariance **is** the Cramér–Rao bound on the drift curve κ(t) and its rate. We drift the **ESD (TST) stage** — the one whose strength really wanders in an interferometer, as charge builds on the reaction mass — with a 5 %, hour-scale profile, on the coupled reduced-quad plant (the ruler `H_stage/H_pcal = κ_i·D_i·N_i` recovers κ through the M0-damped compliance and the nested-offload distribution). ::: {#f7046ab3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Run the campaign — snapshot the drift, fit κ(t)"} c = dd.campaign(seed=777) ``` ::: ## Tracking the drift The injected truth, the per-record snapshots with their error bars, and the recovered κ(t) with its CRB band: ::: {#6e2dad2f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="κ(t): injected truth, snapshots ± σ, LP fit ± CRB"} dd.drift_fig(c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The fit rides straight through the snapshots and follows the injected drift — a 5 % excursion resolved cleanly, even though each single snapshot only pins κ to about a percent. ## Is the recovery honest? A curve through points is easy; a curve that knows its own uncertainty is the point. The recovery residual (recovered − truth) stays inside the ±σ Cramér–Rao band — the error bar neither collapses (which would be fabricated confidence) nor balloons (which would be uselessly conservative): ::: {#3fee8a2d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Tracking error vs the CRB band"} dd.tracking_error_fig(c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## The feasibility gate: is the drift resolvable? Before calling a drift "trackable" or "buried in noise," compute the bound. The tracking σ from the fit is far below the injected drift amplitude, so the drift is genuinely **resolved**, not noise — and the local-stationarity approximation costs a fraction of a percent, well under the per-snapshot error: ::: {#ae3f1b3d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Resolvability — a computed bound, not an eyeball"} display(dd.resolvability_table(c)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Feasibility gate — the injected drift is resolvable (a computed bound, not an eyeball)** | feasibility quantity | value | note | | --- | --- | --- | | injected drift amplitude | 0.0500 | 5% of κ | | per-snapshot σ_κ (median) | 0.0011 | 0.11% of κ | | tracking σ_κ (LP fit, median) | 0.0006 | 0.06% of κ | | resolve ratio = amp / tracking σ | 88× | ≫ 1 ⇒ drift resolved, not noise | | local-stationarity error | 0.22% | record ÷ drift timescale — the approximation cost | ::: ::: The resolve ratio is a knob, not a limit: more periods per snapshot, more snapshots, or a stronger drive all buy it down further — the same Fisher levers as everywhere else in the pipeline. ## The new physics: a drifting SRC detuning δ(t) The coupled plant lets us track the drift that the old single-pole twin could not represent: the **SRC detuning δ**. As the SRC error point wanders around its slightly-detuned operating point, the cavity pole moves — splitting toward a complex pair — and the sensing shape changes with it. δ is a *sensing* parameter, so it does **not** cancel in the κ ruler; instead it is recovered from the **Pcal FRF shape** (`C_meas = H_pcal·(1+G)`), which makes the δ snapshot independent of the κ drift — the two compose into a joint κ(t), δ(t) picture. We drift δ by 5 % around a 5° operating point: ::: {#219ed5ee .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Snapshot the drifting SRC detuning δ(t) from the Pcal FRF, fit δ(t)"} cd = dd.campaign_delta(seed=778) dd.delta_drift_fig(cd) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#05a8fef8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="δ(t) resolvability — a computed bound"} display(dd.delta_resolvability_table(cd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **SRC-detuning drift is resolvable — δ tracked from the Pcal FRF, independent of the κ drift (the two snapshots compose).** | feasibility quantity | value | note | | --- | --- | --- | | injected drift amplitude | 0.2500° | 5% of δ | | per-snapshot σ_δ (median) | 0.0017° | 0.03% of δ | | tracking σ_δ (LP fit, median) | 0.0009° | 0.02% of δ | | resolve ratio = amp / tracking σ | 288× | ≫ 1 ⇒ drift resolved, not noise | | local-stationarity error | 0.22% | record ÷ drift timescale | ::: ::: The detuning is recovered to a hundredth of a degree per snapshot — the coupled-cavity split leaves a strong high-frequency signature in `C`, so δ is well-identified even at this small detuning. Note the separation of concerns: κ comes from the stage/Pcal *ratio* (immune to sensing drift), δ from the Pcal *shape* (immune to actuation drift), so a real interferometer's simultaneous κ- and δ-drift are tracked by two independent snapshots on the same records. ## Round 2: everything drifts at once, and at random The two sections above each drift **one** parameter along a **smooth** curve. Reality is messier on both counts: several calibration numbers wander **simultaneously**, and the wander is **random** (a meandering walk), not a tidy sine. Here we do both — the optical gain `κ_C`, the SRC detuning `δ`, and the ESD strength `κ_ESD` all drift together as random (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck) walks, and each record is fit for **all three at once**. A joint fit is essential because the parameters are not independent: a wobble in one can masquerade as a wobble in another, and only a joint fit — with the Pcal record pinning the sensing and each stage record pinning its own strength — untangles them. ::: {#0c596676 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Three random drifts at once, recovered in one joint fit per record"} cj = dd.campaign_joint(seed=2024) dd.joint_drift_fig(cj) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: All three random wanders are followed within their error bars. The **correlation matrix** of a single snapshot shows *how well* they separate: ::: {#2e6dbaa8 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Which drifts are hard to tell apart"} dd.joint_corr_fig(cj) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `δ` separates cleanly from the two gains (near-zero correlation) — it lives in the sensing *shape*, which the amplitudes don't touch. But `κ_C` (optical gain) and `κ_ESD` (test-mass drive) are strongly **anti-correlated**: both simply scale the ESD line, so the loop shape alone cannot tell an optical-gain change from an actuation change — it is the **Pcal absolute reference** that breaks the tie (exactly why Pcal is the fiducial in a real calibration). The joint fit surfaces that degeneracy honestly rather than hiding it in a one-at-a-time recovery. ## Designing the drive: a few optimal lines, not broadband The rounds above inject a **broadband** multisine — power in every bin — which is *not* how a real calibration drives the interferometer, and *not* what optimal excitation calls for. The plant is **one** system (the opto-mechanical DARM sensing `C` plus the quad suspension) with **one** joint parameter vector, and it is read out by a **few always-on calibration lines**. The right question is where to *put* those lines. Given a prior on how much each parameter drifts, we place and weight a handful of lines — Pcal lines plus one per in-band stage — to **minimise the joint estimator variance on the drifts** (a Bayesian A-optimal design), under the **real force budgets**: the Pcal's ±200 mW photon-calibrator range, and each suspension stage capped at the same displacement ruler. Every line informs every parameter — a suspension line passes through `C` and `1/(1+G)` so it carries sensing information, and the Pcal ruler, compared against a suspension line, carries actuation information — so the design works on the **coupled** Fisher matrix, not two separate problems. ::: {#7b217bad .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Design the A-optimal cal-line roster and score it against a broadband drive"} dc = dd.design_campaign() dd.design_fig(dc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#f4d248af .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Per-parameter drift prior, snapshot σ, and the resolvability margin"} display(dd.design_table(dc)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **A-optimal designed drive: joint cost 0.002 vs 2.032 for a broadband multisine of the same budget (lower = better; max = 4 means the lines add nothing). Every drift is resolved (margin > 1). κ_C's prior is measured (Sun 2020); the others are representative placeholders.** | parameter | drift prior (1σ) | snapshot σ | margin | prior source | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | κ_C (optical gain) | 2.0% | 4.59e-05 | 435× | Sun 2020 (measured 1–2 %) | | δ (SRC detuning) | 1.15° | 6.67e-04 | 30× | representative placeholder | | κ_PUM (L2 drive) | 2.0% | 4.76e-05 | 421× | representative placeholder | | κ_ESD (test-mass drive) | 2.0% | 4.50e-04 | 44× | representative placeholder | ::: ::: The designed handful of lines reaches a far lower joint cost than a broadband multisine of the same budget — the drive belongs where the parameters are informative, not spread thin. Injecting exactly this roster on the twin and reading it back leakage-free recovers the drifting parameters: ::: {#182c5a45 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Track the joint set from the DESIGNED cal-line readout (not broadband)"} tc = dd.tracked_lines_campaign() dd.tracked_lines_fig(tc) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## What's grounded, and what the scope is The **κ_C drift prior is measured** (Sun et al. 2020: the optical gain varies 1–2 % over a run); the **Pcal budget is real** (±200 mW → `pcal_range_disp`); the **O4 line frequencies are published** (Wade et al. 2025, Fig. 4). The drift priors for `δ`, `κ_PUM`, `κ_ESD` are **representative placeholders** — the O3/O4 papers do not quantify them — and the per-stage force caps are **derived** by matching the Pcal ruler, since the papers give no per-stage line amplitude. The design tracks the **identifiable joint set** for this twin and the O4 floor: `κ_C`, `δ`, and the two in-band stages `κ_PUM`/`κ_ESD`. The other TDCFs are feasibility-gated, not hidden: **`κ_M0`** is the *top mass*, offloaded below ~0.5 Hz, so its line falls outside the ≥10 Hz band the O4 floor covers; and **`f_cc`/`τ`** need a wideband high-frequency Pcal spread to become well-conditioned. The joint Fisher (`darm_callines.joint_fisher`) quantifies exactly what each of those would require. ::: ## Honest gaps On the coupled reduced-quad plant, the machinery now tracks **several parameters drifting at once, under a realistic random wander, within a Cramér–Rao bound, from a P&S-optimal designed cal-line drive** — and the correlation matrix names the degeneracies instead of hiding them. What's still simplified: the random walk is a plain Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (a Gaussian-process wander with a measured drift spectrum is the honest next step); the estimator is the two-step form (snapshot, then basis-fit) rather than the one-shot Lataire–Pintelon fit; the drift priors for all but `κ_C` are representative placeholders pending real per-parameter numbers; and `κ_M0`, `f_cc`, `τ` need the out-of-band / wideband lines noted above to join the tracked set. What this page establishes is the foundation: the "can we track it?" question gets a numeric answer, jointly, from an optimal drive, and honestly — see `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`.
